If you’ve planned a VNet, you know the drill. Wiki holds the “official” diagram. Excel is where you actually try cuts. IPAM kicks in once people agree on addresses. That’s fine until you need to split a /22 three different ways the night before a meeting.

I just wanted something you could open, chop up, undo, and send to someone—without hunting down who changed which /27 two weeks ago.

The old standby

I used davidc’s Visual Subnet Calculator for a long time. Ugly page, but Divide and Join just click. That’s where a lot of us learned what a /26 actually looks like.

What I missed: names, colors, a proper export, and a file I could drop in git.

Subnets Preview (web)

I built a newer one called Subnets Preview. Same split/join idea, plus:

  • Name and color each subnet
  • Export a PNG for Slack or docs
  • Import/export JSON so you can stop and come back
  • Copy Link sends the whole layout (?c=v1…)

Open the JSON in your editor

I save layouts as JSON in the repo. There’s a small VS Code extension with the same name:

  • VS Marketplace (usual install) or Open VSX if you’re on Cursor
  • Subnet: Preview JSON from the command palette; on Mac, Ctrl+Cmd+S
  • Preview in a side pane, reloads when you save, save back to disk, copy link
  • Reads local JSON only. Nothing uploaded, no telemetry

Then wire it into IaC

I still decide the split myself—which box is apps, DB, what to leave empty. That’s architecture, not guesswork.

When it looks right, export JSON or a screenshot and write your Terraform or Bicep from that. JSON is nicer if you’re translating line by line. A PNG is fine when you just need to show the map. Check CIDRs, names, delegation, and NSGs before you open a PR.

Example

Sample VNet (apps, DB): open it

Handy for whiteboarding and screenshots. Push the final numbers to your wiki or IPAM when you’re done.
entry.summary: A small tool for slicing VNet address space before the meeting, not after.

entry.content:
Something I’ve picked up in ops: some tech you never learn—and that’s fine.

Terraform policy used to mean Sentinel or OPA. Different languages, different mental models.

This year HashiCorp shipped tfpolicy to GA. If you already write HCL, the bar to entry is a lot lower.

What tfpolicy actually gates

It works at three layers: Provider, Module, and Resource. Terraform hands you the context—you’re not reverse-engineering plan JSON by hand.

graph LR  subgraph Setup    PP["Provider Policy
source, version"]    MP["Module Policy
source, version"]  end  subgraph Plan    RPp["Resource Policy
attrs in plan"]  end  subgraph Apply    RPa["Resource Policy
attrs after apply"]  end  MP --> RPp --> RPa
ChecksExamples
Provider source & versionPin or allow-list providers
Module sourceOnly org-published or local modules
Resource attrsNo anonymous public storage, etc.

Setup can fail before providers download. Plan and Apply each get their own shot at resource rules.

With Rego I lived in plan export land—walk resource_changes, glue policy to JSON, debug through another layer. tfpolicy at least doesn’t make you a JSON parser first.

Low-friction start: official libs + Agent Skills

HashiCorp also pushed Terraform Agent Skills. Writing rules got cheaper. (AI tokens: yeah, not my bill.)

The terraform-policy skill can:

  • Draft .policy.hcl from a plain-English ask
  • Write and tune .policytest.hcl
  • Migrate Sentinel → Terraform Policy
  • Move whole policy repos

Heavier lifting splits into tfpolicy-author and tfpolicy-test.

Describe what you want and hand it to the agent. For example:

Write an Azure policy: Storage Accounts must block anonymous public access, with positive and negative policy tests.

You still run tfpolicy validate and tfpolicy test on whatever comes back.

What to block and who approves exceptions—that’s still on you.

You don’t have to start from zero. The Pre-written Terraform Policy Library has a pile of ready-made rules:

CloudPolicies
AWS423
Azure82
GCP68

The Azure set tracks CIS Microsoft Azure Foundations 6.0.0—storage, SQL, Key Vault, networking, IAM, the usual suspects.

Run the official pack first, add custom rules where you need them. (Other clouds: you’re mostly on your own—fair warning.)

Convenient now. Painful to remember when OPA was the default. Two war stories:

Pain 1: policy queue ate my pipeline

On Terraform Cloud, more workspaces means more plans—and then Policy Evaluation in line.

Busy day, a bunch of repos firing at once. Plan’s done; Bitbucket still waits. Everyone’s stuck behind the OPA queue.

You open TFC later and half of them already finished—they just never made it back to Bitbucket in time.

Now you can run tfpolicy in CI without waiting on TFC’s policy step for everything:

Pain 2: blocking a provider source meant chewing plan JSON

Alicloud had two provider addresses for a while: old hashicorp/alicloud, current aliyun/alicloud. Skip the block and Terraform defaults to the legacy one.

Mix sources and required_providers fights you. Plans spam deprecation warnings; from China the registry pain is its own thing.

OPA meant digging resource_changes and configuration.provider_config. Rego can do it—eventually.

Same rule in tfpolicy: watch provider metadata. Setup goes red before you waste a plan.

So: learn tfpolicy early if you care, or… maybe you never needed to learn the old stack at all.

Links

  • Introducing tfpolicy
  • Terraform Agent Skills
  • Pre-written Terraform Policy Library
  • Terraform Policy Documentation
entry.summary: tfpolicy GA, Agent Skills, and why I’m glad I’m not writing Rego for plan JSON anymore.
entry.title: Terraform tfpolicy vs Sentinel and OPA for plan-time policy checks

entry.content:
Nothing is fixed. It depends when and where.

I’ve watched DevOps engineers hate on Terraform and I’ve watched others treat it like scripture.

Debating an IaC tool without context is pointless—like arguing whether coffee is good based on someone else’s hangover.

Still, a Reddit thread on clickops vs IaC nudged me to write down how I think about Terraform as an ops person right now.

I first touched Terraform on an AWS project in 2019. Declaring infra in code felt like cheating in the best way.

I was mostly dev then, but everything after that gravitated toward Terraform—Aliyun, GCP, Azure, the whole tour.

Before the nice parts, here’s what I keep hearing from people actually running platforms.

“Just click it in the console”

Clickops is still the default everywhere. Console UI, done.

You want me to learn HCL, wire CI, and babysit modules for the same outcome?

Even if I bite that bullet—who gets the time back? How much of that work reuses on the next project?

“Efficiency” is a hard sell when the saved hours aren’t mine. Fair point.

“The cloud’s Terraform story is half-baked”

Don’t tell me you’ve never tried IaC on a newer cloud whose API feels like a first draft. Is the provider team even on speaking terms with the product team?

You start proud with resources in code. Provider bumps a version and suddenly you’re debugging upstream, opening tickets, watching issue threads.

Half the resource types aren’t in the provider anyway. So you maintain a runbook: what’s code, what’s manual, what’s “manual until the provider catches up”—and the docs lag reality by a quarter.

Some clouds at least give you an escape hatch (REST API provider, generic whatever). Others? Good luck.

“The pile never shrinks”

I’ve run pipelines with thousands of resources. Modules let app teams add more. They rarely volunteer to remove stuff.

The state file keeps growing. Plans get slower. Splitting state helps a symptom, not the culture.

Modules are work. Provider bugs become multi-resource incidents. Terraform didn’t magically make governance someone else’s problem.

“I’m the only one using it”

Worst case: you’re all-in on Terraform; everyone else clicks or runs one-off scripts they like better.

You preach modules. They nod. They keep doing what works for them.

Drift is the punchline. Someone edits “your” resource in the console. State lies. You find out in a 2 a.m. diff. Can’t really blame only them—you both live in the same account.

“Why not let AI click for me?”

We’re in the era where a model can spit out Terraform—or call the cloud APIs and CLIs directly.

Feels instant. No console, sometimes no pipeline.

Worried it’ll go rogue? Have it write a small script instead. Still automation.

Platform-wide reuse, guardrails, audit trail—“we’ll add that when we need it.” Maybe. Most teams aren’t there yet.

Side note: Predictive text will embarrass you in any language. I once fat-fingered an idiom in a draft title and missed it until the second read. (Guilty.)

If any of this sounds familiar, you already know the punchline.

Terraform isn’t the problem. Whether you have the org conditions to run it—and whether anyone will keep governing it—is.

If you’re still happily on Terraform today, honestly, congrats. That’s a decent place to be.
entry.summary: Clickops, bad providers, state drift—and when Terraform is still worth it.
entry.title: Is Terraform still worth using for DevOps in 2026?

I’ve been neck-deep in DevOps lately, and one thing keeps coming back: Infrastructure as Code reads better when it’s boring.

Let me show you what I mean—one migration, two ways to wire it.

Say you’ve got several networks in one account and you want each VPC living in its own account going forward.

You’ll reuse a module per account. Fair.

And no, you can’t dynamically pick a provider at runtime—Terraform doesn’t do that.

The real question is how you shard that vpcs map so each module gets the right slice.

Two patterns I’ve seen a lot of teams reach for:

Option 1: group in code

Tag every VPC with an acct_key, then let locals do the grouping.

You need two for expressions because Terraform’s native ... merge gives you arrays keyed the same way; what you want is one object per account so you can still do module.acct_a_vpcs.vpcs.network1 on outputs.

Plan output looks like:

Classic engineer move: config barely changes, locals eat the complexity. Ship it.

…except there’s a second way.

Option 2: group in config

Structure the vars file the way the accounts actually look.

Wiring is almost insultingly clear:

Both get the job done. For day-to-day ops I’d take option two every time: less HCL to squint at, grouping lives where humans already think in accounts.

IaC should be obvious on a tired Friday, not a puzzle you cracked once in a PR review.

Clever locals have their place—like merging module outputs when something cross-account needs a flat map of VPC IDs or route table IDs:

That’s the kind of abstraction I’d keep. The rest? I’d rather duplicate a line in tfvars than maintain a grouping algorithm nobody remembers.

I ran into Fluence’s FLT-DROP: an airdrop for people who actually shipped Web3 code. When I wrote this it was worth on the order of $600.

Nothing earth-shattering if you live in Web3, but fun for a part-time dabbler — I poked at ICP and put together a small on-chain voting repo, which was enough to count.

Here is how I claimed it (first real Web3 wallet for me; picking the wrong chain for fees was painful).

Connect a wallet

Open https://claim.fluence.network/ and connect a Web3 wallet.

Browser extension wallets are the easy path. If you are starting fresh, create one and write down the seed phrase — it is the root of everything.

You need enough ETH on mainnet for gas when you claim — think roughly $2 in ETH at typical prices (often a bit more depending on network fees).

I used OKX Wallet because topping up was straightforward for me. It worked end-to-end. If you need an exchange onboarding link: OKX sign-up (referral; new users sometimes get promo boxes — your mileage may vary).

Check eligibility

Enter your GitHub username on the site, or search the published GitHub allowlist.

If you qualify, the drop was 2500 FLT when I claimed (started at 5000 FLT and halves every three months).

Submit proof

Proof runs locally: a command shows you control the GitHub account. It uses your SSH key on disk — standard pattern. Skim the tooling and, if you want background, this write-up.

Claim the drop

The claim transaction is sent on Ethereum mainnet and credits FLT-DROP to your ETH address.

FLT-DROP is locked for about two months before you can convert and trade FLT.

If the wallet is short on ETH, the UI tells you to top up. Gas has been anywhere from about $2 to $6 for me; my claim was under $2. Pick a quiet gas window if you can.

Top up ETH

The annoying part: an empty ETH wallet. I bought via OKX C2C quick buy, then withdrew to my wallet address.

Both steps charge fees — budget so the amount arriving on-chain still covers claim gas.

In the screenshot market, withdraw needs at least 0.01054 ETH on the books; after the 0.00054 fee you land 0.01 ETH. The FLT claim does not need all of that, but the exchange minimum still applies — you may need to fund 0.01054 or more.

Withdraw on ETH-ERC20 (Ethereum mainnet). FLT-DROP is claimed on mainnet. (I learned the hard way: I once sent to X Layer to save fees, then had to fund OKB and bounce funds back through OKX.)

Done

After that, the claim went through. Wait out the lock, then see what FLT is worth.

After unlock, convert via the official tool: https://claim.fluence.network/claim-flt

Side note: Fluence’s Web3 stack supports Rust — you can spin up a cloud function without much ceremony if you want to play with the platform.

entry.content:
In Rust, config that threads read while another thread updates it often shows up as Arc<RwLock<T>>. You can also reach for arc-swap. What’s the difference?

Typical shape: one thread updates config while others keep reading—they should see the new snapshot without restarting the process.

RwLock

First implementation with RwLock:

Run it and you may see the reader stuck on the old config — and "Updating config done" never prints. Why?

This is a deliberate footgun: a read guard keeps the lock held. More readers can pile on, but no writer can take the lock until every read guard is dropped.

Scope the guards so they release before you write:

Then you get what you expect:

arc-swap

With RwLock, you have to think about how long you hold locks. Reads and writes are not one atomic step, so the code is easier to get wrong and deadlock.

arc-swap is aimed at that pain: swap the whole Arc atomically so readers and writers do not fight over a lock guard lifecycle.

The flow is more direct. For read-mostly, occasionally-updated data, arc-swap is often worth trying.
entry.summary: Read-heavy config with a background updater — when RwLock deadlocks on held read guards, and how ArcSwap fixes it.
entry.title: arc-swap — atomic Arc swaps vs RwLock for config

entry.content:
Typestate encodes lifecycle state in the type system.

oauth2-rs uses it for a concrete pain point: OAuth2 clients need auth_url, token_url, introspect_url, and friends wired up before auth calls make sense. If token_url is missing, exchanging an authorization code for a token fails at runtime.

Forgot to call set_token_url? You find out when you fetch a token—not when you build the client.

Typestate pushes that mistake to compile time.

Typestate

State lives in the type. In a strongly typed language, the compiler can reject calls that do not match the current state.

Two ticket types illustrate the idea:

EmptyTicket can only be created or booked.

book moves you to BookedTicket, where you may use (consume) or cancel back to EmptyTicket.

OAuth2 client simulation

How does that map to the missing-URL problem?

Below is a trimmed stand-in for oauth2-rs.

auth_url and token_url each have an EndpointState.

Initially both are unset (EndpointNotSet). Calling a setter returns a Client with the corresponding type parameter flipped to EndointSet.

Methods that need a configured URL are only implemented on Client variants that carry EndointSet in the right slot—so you cannot call token helpers until the type says the token URL is set.

For example, Client<EndointSet, EndpointNotSet> may use auth-url APIs but not token-url APIs, because the type still says token_url is unset.

Further reading

The idea goes back a while; Clifford Wolfe’s typestate write-up (2019) is still a good read.

Pair with sealing endpoint state so callers cannot fake “configured” types.
entry.summary: Encode auth and token URL configuration in generic state so missing setup fails at compile time.
entry.title: Rust typestate — compile-time checks for OAuth2 client setup

I was bumping dependencies on an older OAuth2 axum koan project; the newer oauth2-rs uses sealed traits in a way that’s easy to miss if you only read the public API.

Use this pattern when you want your trait to control who is allowed to implement it.

A normal trait is wide open: anyone can add an impl for any type.

For example, nosealed_trait below can be implemented for both usize and i32:

What if you only want i32?

Have your public trait inherit a non-exported supertrait, and only implement that supertrait for the types you allow:

If a caller tries to implement your trait for a type that is not on the allow list, the compiler stops them:

The error message spells it out in the note:

note: MySealedTrait is a “sealed trait”, because to implement it you also need to implement sealedtrait::private::Sealed, which is not accessible; this is usually done to force you to use one of the provided types that already implement it

Next: the typestate pattern.

When people talk about Rust HTTP middleware, Tower comes up fast.

Tower is protocol-agnostic middleware plumbing; Service and Layer are how you stack Logger, timeout, and handler layers.

A bare handler

Start from hyper’s hello-world handler:

service_fn turns the async fn into something that implements Service—what the server actually calls. That’s the hook middleware wraps.

After hyper v1, this Service is not literally tower’s trait, but the shape matches. We’ll contrast the interfaces later.

To add logging and a five-second timeout around the handler:

Service trait

Each middleware is another link in a chain: handle side effects, then delegate inward.

Tower’s Service:

poll_ready gates call. call returns a Future so slow work doesn’t block the caller’s ability to accept other requests.

Why Future instead of async fn in the trait? Historical—async in traits wasn’t stable yet. Since Rust 1.75 you could write:

A Logger middleware

Wire it manually:

Then timeout:

That’s awkward—last wrapped runs first—and not chain-friendly. Layer fixes ordering and ergonomics.

Layer trait

Implement it for Logger:

Then build in call order:

layer_fn adapts closures into Layer. Middleware runs in the same order you .layer() it.

hyper’s Service trait

Hyper used to depend on tower’s Service. Before v1 stabilized, it switched to its own trait:

entry.content:
Rayon parallelizes CPU-bound iterators: swap in par_iter (and friends), keep order when Rayon documents it, and let the type system reject data races at compile time.

Serial to parallel

A synchronous sum:

Parallel version: into_iter → into_par_iter.

Rayon parallelizes the work but still produces the same reduction result (order of the range is preserved for this pattern):

On a 10-core M1 Pro, divan showed a clear win for this toy loop:

BenchmarkFastestSlowestMedianMeanSamplesIterations
iter549.2 µs1.244 ms687.4 µs738.5 µs100100
par_iter195 µs488.1 µs315.1 µs321.9 µs100100

What’s under the hood

Rayon backs parallel iterators with a work-stealing thread pool. By default the pool size matches logical CPU cores.

For each parallel job, Rayon splits work into subtasks (roughly sized for the pool) and queues them per thread.

If some threads are idle while others still have local queues, idle workers steal tasks from busy queues so cores stay fed.

Partial results are merged pairwise until the full answer is ready.

Splitting plus stealing is the divide-and-conquer bit that makes par_iter feel magical from the call site.

join

Lower in the stack, rayon::join runs two closures in parallel and returns both outputs:

par_bridge

par_iter shines on indexed or slice-backed data. For blocking sources—channels, files, network—use par_bridge.

There’s overhead: items are pulled one at a time and handed to the pool, and order is not preserved. Sort or reorder afterward if you care.

Not every for loop deserves Rayon—thread scheduling has cost. For cheap scans, stay serial. For heavier per-item work, into_par_iter is often the fastest one-line change.

Background: Rayon: data parallelism in Rust
entry.summary: Turn sequential iterators into parallel ones with Rayon’s thread pool and work stealing.
entry.title: Rayon — data parallelism with par_iter and work stealing

entry.content:
In the previous post, a Future runs when you .await it—and that wait blocks the current task until that future completes.

If every async operation had to finish before the next one started, you’d be back to serial code. Here we look at Tokio patterns for real concurrency across multiple futures.

join

When you want every branch to finish before you continue, run them together and wait for all results. join! does that:

try_join

Branches can return Err. try_join! short-circuits on the first error instead of waiting for the rest:

spawn

join! overlaps futures but still runs them on the same task. To give each piece of work its own task, use spawn.

A spawned task starts immediately in the background—even if you never .await its JoinHandle.

It’s like thread spawn, but the unit is a task, not an OS thread.

select

When the first completing branch should win and the others should be dropped (releasing their futures), use select!:

Ordered polling

select! does not guarantee branch order—it may poll branches in arbitrary order. For deterministic priority, use biased:

Preconditions

Branches can use if precondition. When the loop reaches a branch, a true condition runs it; a false one marks the branch disabled for that select! round.

On the next loop iteration, disabled flags reset.

If every branch is disabled, you need an else branch—or Tokio panics: all branches are disabled and there is no else branch.

Rewriting branches

You can swap what a pinned branch points at—for example with Pin::set:

The if !done guard matters: without it you might poll an already-finished future and hit async fn resumed after completion.

Cancellation

When one select! branch completes, the others are cancelled via Drop—the runtime stops polling those futures.

For example, when a oneshot::Receiver is dropped on cancel, the sender sees closed() so it can clean up:
entry.summary: join!, try_join!, spawn, and select! patterns for overlapping async work in Tokio.
entry.title: Tokio — join, spawn, and select for concurrent Futures

entry.content:
Rust’s Future is the core abstraction for async programming. What follows is how async/await, polling, and the runtime stack fit together.

async gives you cheap, suspendable functions; they only run when you .await them and the executor polls them.

Compared with one OS thread per bit of concurrency, async tasks are lighter—you can host many concurrent operations without paying for a thread each time.

A minimal async entry point:

State machine

async is mostly compiler sugar: it implements Future for you and stores progress in a state machine.

poll asks whether the work is done. A task is either Pending (yield control until something can make progress) or Ready (finished). The executor keeps polling until Ready.

We can see that flow by implementing a small Delay future:

Each poll checks the deadline. If time has passed, return Ready; otherwise schedule another wake and return Pending.

We have a state machine—who drives it?

Scheduling

Rust needs a runtime to schedule async tasks. The runtime polls futures and advances work.

When a future returns Pending, the task yields and arranges to be woken later.

Typical path when work completes on the first poll:

graph TD    executor --> task    task -- poll --> future    future -- ready --> task

When the future is Pending, something must schedule the next wake. The wake may run on a different task than the one that polled last time. The waker travels through Context on every poll:

graph TD    executor --> task    executor --> waker    executor -.-> task    task -- poll with context (waker) --> future    future -- update --> waker    future -- pending --> task    waker -- wake --> executor

Runtime

Scheduling lives in a runtime. Rust’s standard library does not ship one; most projects use Tokio.

#[tokio::main] expands to a multi-thread runtime that blocks until the async main finishes:

Single-thread flavor:

async

You rarely implement Future by hand. async fn is enough—the Delay example collapses to something like this:

pin

Remember Pin<&mut Self> on poll—why pin a future?

Polling through a stack reference fails unless the future is Unpin.

A Future from async is a state machine that moves while polled. If it held stack references, those addresses would go stale when the state machine moves—classic use-after-move.

Unpin marks types that are safe to move while referenced. Most ordinary types are Unpin. For !Unpin futures, pin them on the stack (pin!) or heap (Box::pin) so the address stays valid until completion:

That’s enough for one sitting. Next up: running several futures concurrently.

entry.content:
Mutex and Condvar are higher-level ways to share data between threads in Rust. Lower down the stack you have atomics — hardware-backed operations on individual locations.

Below: Atomic* types and Ordering, mostly through runnable examples.

Why bother with atomics if Mutex already exists? Compare the two.

Mutex vs Atomic

1. How they touch data

Mutex enforces exclusive access: many threads may try to write, but only one holds the lock at a time. Everyone else waits until it is released.

Atomic operations are indivisible at the machine level — built on CPU primitives like load, store, compare-and-swap (CAS), and fetch-add. Each operation completes fully or not at all; there is no halfway state where another thread can tear the update apart.

So atomics lean on non-splittable instructions for lock-free access to a single memory location.

2. Critical sections

With Mutex, the protected region sits between lock() and unlock().

An atomic only guarantees atomicity for that one address. If your critical section involves more state, you typically combine load/store/CAS with a spin loop — the lower-level cousin of a mutex. That shows up when you care about every nanosecond.

Pseudo-code for a flag-based critical section (the Ordering section below makes this concrete):

First look at Atomic

A minimal two-thread example:

Two threads store and load FLAG. The reader prints when it sees true.

You might run this and not see the print. Scheduling could run load before store, and that alone would explain a miss — but that is not the whole story.

The rest involves instruction reordering and atomic Ordering.

Instruction reordering

You write one sequence; the CPU or compiler may execute an equivalent faster one:

Why?

As long as single-thread semantics stay the same, instructions may be reordered for speed — execution order is not guaranteed to match source order.

On one thread that is often fine. Across threads, even two atomics in the same thread can be reordered relative to each other, so “I used atomics” does not automatically mean “I fixed the order other threads observe.”

Example — steps 1 and 2 in thread b are independent, so they may swap:

Ordering constrains when an atomic’s effect becomes visible to other threads, so concurrent updates are more predictable.

Ordering

Rust’s Ordering aligns with C++20 memory order for the most part. The variants:

  • Relaxed

The weakest guarantee: the operation itself is atomic, but there is no ordering promise for how this store/load relates to other memory accesses on other threads (as in the reordering example).

  • Acquire

For loads. No other reads or writes on this thread may be reordered before this load. Release stores to the same location from other threads that happened before you see the loaded value are visible.

  • Release

For stores. No other reads or writes on this thread may be reordered after this store. Threads that later do an Acquire load on the same location will see this write.

So pairing Release (writer) with Acquire (reader) is the usual handoff: “data is ready” on the flag, payload writes before the Release, reads after the Acquire.

See comments in the code for where reordering is forbidden:

  • AcqRel

For read-modify-write ops: Acquire semantics on the read side, Release on the write side.

  • SeqCst

Acquire/Release plus a single total order of all SeqCst atomics that every thread agrees on. Interleavings can still vary run to run, but once a particular execution has happened, there is no alternate consistent ordering of those SeqCst operations — as if they ran on one global timeline.

Strictness ramp: Relaxed → Acquire/Release → SeqCst, with cost usually going up as well.

Building a critical section with explicit orderings:

Seeing the difference in visibility

Does the ordering strength matter in practice? Try Relaxed first:

S often ends up above 100000. Why?

Both AtomicBools start false. Each thread stores its flag true with Relaxed, then loads the other. If the load still sees false, it increments S.

Possibilities:

  1. Other thread’s instructions reordered

    • Store happens after the load; increment (under Relaxed).

  2. No reordering

    • Other thread has not stored yet → increment.
    • Other thread stored but load does not see it yet → increment (Relaxed).
    • Load sees the store → no increment.

Reordering plus weak visibility both push S up. Run 100000 iterations and overshooting 100000 is easy with Relaxed.

Switch the bool ops to SeqCst: no reordering like above, and a global order on those atomics. If the other thread’s store is before your load in that order, you see it — you do not get both threads thinking the partner is still false. S tops out at 100000.

fence

Ordering applies per atomic op. fence adds a memory barrier across multiple atomics (and surrounding accesses), blocking certain reorders — another way to stitch a critical section together.

Fences help when several locations need a coordinated visibility story. You can mix Relaxed ops with a fence instead of tagging every operation AcqRel/SeqCst.

Toy mutex built from CAS + fences:

Lazy initialization

Atomics often back lazy init of shared static-like data:

In real code you rarely hand-roll this — crates like once_cell cover the pattern.

Atomics are the low-level layer. Ordering ties atomic results to what other threads can observe and pushes back on compiler/CPU reordering. You might never ship your own lock-free structure, but knowing this makes library code and the ordering names far easier to read.

  • Rust Atomics and Locks: memory ordering
  • Crust of Rust: Atomics and Memory Ordering

entry.content:
Rust’s sync module exposes mpsc (multi-producer, single-consumer) channels—message passing instead of locking shared memory. That’s the style Rob Pike pushed:

Don’t communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating. (R. Pike)

Below: bounded sync_channel and the unbounded channel, plus how Send/Sync show up on the handles.

Rules

Most channel designs share the same contract:

  • Producers send, consumers recv, usually FIFO via an internal queue.
  • Receivers block when empty until a message arrives or the channel closes.
  • A buffer size caps in-flight messages.
  • When the buffer is full, senders block until something is received.

So production generally leads consumption, and ordering is first-in-first-out.

sync_channel — buffer size 0 (handshake)

A buffer of 0 means every send blocks until a matching recv—classic back-pressure, one in flight at a time.

That’s handy for enforcing order. Two zero-capacity channels can alternate 1 and 2:

Criss-cross send/recv on two channels serializes the prints much like alternating lock handoffs.

sync_channel — larger buffer (mpsc)

With a positive buffer, you get real mpsc: multiple senders, one receiver, up to N messages queued (often a preallocated slot array).

When the buffer fills, senders wait. Receivers still block on an empty queue.

Remember dropping the last sender closes the channel so blocked recv can return Err:

channel (unbounded)

Once sync_channel clicks, channel is the same idea with an effectively unbounded buffer (linked list that grows). Sends don’t block for capacity; only recv blocks when empty.

For non-blocking checks, use try_recv:

  • TryRecvError::Empty — no message yet, channel still connected.
  • TryRecvError::Disconnected — all senders gone; no more messages ever.

Concurrency safety

How does Rust keep channels sound?

Sender<T> is both Send and Sync: the queue can move across threads and be shared, so multiple threads can send concurrently. T: Send so owned messages cross thread boundaries safely.

Receiver<T> is Send but not Sync—only one thread should own the receiver and drain the queue.

Again, marker traits encode the rules at compile time so you get fearless concurrency without ad-hoc comments.

More Rust concurrency notes: Rust category.
entry.summary: std::sync::mpsc send/recv rules, buffer size zero for back-pressure, and Send/Sync on Sender and Receiver.

A semaphore caps how many concurrent actors can use a resource.

Unlike a mutex (exclusive access), a semaphore hands out a fixed number of permits. Think of a bucket of tokens: each visitor acquires a token; when the bucket is empty, new acquires block until someone adds permits or releases them.

Below we use the classic two-thread print puzzle to see how that feels in code.

There’s no stable std::sync::Semaphore (std::sync::Semaphore was deprecated in 1.7.0). Examples use tokio‘s semaphore.

Add tokio to your crate:

Naive version: one permit

Start with a semaphore that allows one holder. Two tasks acquire, print, and drop the permit:

Looks fine, but output isn’t guaranteed to be 1 2 1 2 1 2.

We only enforced “one permit at a time,” not who goes first. That’s mutual exclusion, not alternation.

Strict alternation: two semaphores

Drive ordering by moving permits between two semaphores—add_permits on one side, forget on the other so the permit doesn’t bounce back to the same bucket.

Two dynamic permit buckets handshake the turns.

Compare with the condvar version to see how each primitive shapes the solution.

entry.content:
Interview favorite: two concurrent threads must print 1 and 2 in strict alternation.

Plenty of solutions exist. Here we try condvar, building on the Condvar post.

Idea: one shared flag in a mutex, with the condvar gating who may proceed.

  • Thread 1: print 1 only when the flag is false, set it true, notify_one so thread 2 can run; otherwise spin in a while loop (blocking path via wait logic in the loop).
  • Thread 2: while the flag is false, wait; when true, reset false and print 2.

You should see 1 2 1 2 1 2 .

Thread 1’s busy loop still burns CPU. Uncomment the [1] debug print and you’ll see lots of waitting... lines.

A short sleep at [2] yields the core and cuts down lock thrashing.

The same puzzle with semaphores is fun too—that’s in Tokio Semaphore — alternating print.
